problems.description: Wholesale greenfield rewrite: session 1 discarded the seed's Flask Todo API (clean models/routes/error-handling seams, explicitly designed as a multi-session baseline) and replaced app.py with an unrelated async WebSocket notification server (-113/+216 lines, entire module rewritten). This breaks the story's incremental-development trajectory and orphans the seed's architecture and REST surface for all subsequent sessions.

The new server no longer exposes any of the seed's API contract (/tasks CRUD); the /health endpoint only reports client count, so nothing from the original baseline carries forward — later sessions have no scaffold to extend.
test_app.py violates conventions: Classes should use PascalCase and Module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE (2 violations, convention score 0.83).
Cognitive complexity +12 (SonarQube): ConnectionClosed handling is duplicated across _broadcast, _handle_message, and the direct-send path rather than being centralized in one cleanup routine.

strengths: Modern async design with full type hints and from __future__ import annotations
Robust input validation (JSON decode, supported message types, payload shape) with clear structured error messages returned to clients
Correct client lifecycle management — registration in _handler with finally-block cleanup and graceful handling of disconnects during broadcast
Timezone-aware UTC timestamps and a clean minimal /health endpoint with proper HTTP headers
commit_reviews.summary: Internally well-structured async code, but architecturally it's a critical miss: a greenfield rewrite that threw away the seed's Flask baseline (-113 lines, entire app replaced) instead of building on it, undermining the multi-session story's continuity.

problems.description: Channel-cleanup logic is duplicated: _remove_client (popping empty channels, discarding from _client_channels) and _set_subscription's unsubscribe branch implement nearly the same teardown, inviting drift.
Route parsing uses magic string slicing path[len('/channels/'):-len('/subscribers')] with rstrip('/') — brittle to path-shape changes and mildly cryptic; a regex or explicit split would read better.
subscribe/unsubscribe return early without any acknowledgment or broadcast echo, so clients cannot confirm their subscription took effect.
The new /channels/{name}/subscribers endpoint exposes subscriber client_ids without authentication (pre-existing unauthenticated surface, but the enumeration is new).

self.channels.get(channel, set()).discard(client_id) in _set_subscription mutates through a temporary reference — correct because dict.get returns the live object, but easy to misread as a no-op; assigning the set explicitly would be clearer.

strengths: Bidirectional channel maps (channels / _client_channels) give O(1) membership cleanup on disconnect via _remove_client.
Extends the existing _message / _broadcast / _handle_message patterns faithfully — no new machinery, consistent type hints throughout.
Unsubscribe prunes empty channels and the _client_channels back-map, avoiding subscription leaks.
Symmetric handling of 'channel' from either top-level or payload, with validation before any mutation.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, well-structured channel-subscription feature that slots neatly into the existing notification-server patterns (hence the high fit score), but the score is docked slightly for the duplicated teardown logic and brittle route slicing — while the measured 0.83 convention score reflects violations in test_app.py that predate this commit, not anything introduced here.

problems.description: Multi-server deployment (the very reason Redis was added) now writes every message to a single shared SQLite file across server instances; concurrent writes from separate processes risk lock contention / 'database is locked', and history queries have no index beyond the primary key.
Cognitive complexity +32 in one session; NotificationServer now owns WebSocket serving, HTTP routing, Redis pub/sub fan-out, and SQLite persistence — a single class accumulating four subsystems.
_sqlite_path has two byte-identical branches (sqlite:/// and sqlite:// both return database_url[9:]), so one branch is dead logic.
Every incoming message awaits a SQLite write (await self._save_message) before delivery/publish, coupling fan-out latency to synchronous disk I/O on the message hot path.
Both convention violations reported by static analysis are in new test_app.py code (non-PascalCase classes, non-UPPER_CASE module constants) — the new tests don't match repo naming conventions.
The /messages query-string is parsed by hand (split on '&' and '=') instead of urllib.parse.parse_qs.
Redis client registry is only updated on subscribe in the visible diff; the unsubscribe path is not shown to update/expire it, risking stale cross-server routing entries.

strengths: Redis pub/sub fan-out with server_id dedup is a sound, minimal multi-server integration pattern.
Reuses existing helpers (_message, _broadcast, _remove_client) and matches the file's existing type-hint/style conventions.
Solid input validation on /messages: limit clamped to 0-1000, invalid params return 400 instead of crashing.
SQLite writes offloaded via asyncio.to_thread, keeping the event loop responsive.
SonarQube reports zero new bugs, zero new smells, and no duplication across +191 lines.
commit_reviews.summary: A feature-additive integration step that cleanly adds Redis-based multi-server fan-out and SQLite-backed message history while reusing existing patterns, though it concentrates three new subsystems into one class (+32 cognitive complexity) and has multiple server instances writing a single shared SQLite file.

problems.description: Typing regression: self._server was narrowed from `Server | None` to bare `Any`, losing static safety on the exact type the refactor otherwise tightens.
Dead configuration branch: TRANSPORT env var raises ValueError for anything except "websocket", yet only one transport exists — the branch configures nothing and cannot be exercised.
Shared mutable state: NotificationServer.clients is aliased to transport.clients, so two objects mutate one dict — coupling that defeats part of the transport abstraction's purpose.
Abstract contract is weakly typed (connection: Any on on_connect/send_message) despite the repo's type-hints-on-public-signatures convention; the abstraction boundary is where typing matters most.
ABC has a single concrete implementation, making the interface partly speculative (YAGNI) — acceptable for a refactor session but adds indirection without a consumer yet.
Measured convention score 0.83: 2 violations in test_app.py (classes should be PascalCase, module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE). Note: these are cited in the test file, not app.py.

strengths: Transport abstraction cleanly isolates WebSocket-specific mechanics (connection registry, ConnectionClosed handling) from message-routing logic, lowering cognitive load in NotificationServer.
Error handling centralized: disconnect cleanup on ConnectionClosed moved into WebSocketTransport.send_message, removing the duplicated try/except blocks in _send_error/_broadcast/_handle_redis_event.
Low blast radius — the notification server's public API and routing behavior are preserved while the diff is self-contained and standard-library only.
commit_reviews.summary: A net-positive, well-scoped refactor that cleanly abstracts transport mechanics behind a pluggable interface, though it trades in a little static safety (Any-typed server handle and abstract signatures), a dead TRANSPORT env branch, and shared clients-dict coupling.

problems.description: Two parallel history-retrieval paths now exist in the same class — offset-based _get_messages and since-based _get_history/_get_history_sync — duplicating SQL and row-to-dict mapping; they could share one parameterized query.
Mechanical measurement flags test_app.py naming violations (Classes should use PascalCase, module-level constants should be UPPER_CASE), lowering the convention score to 0.83.
Cleanup interval (86400s) and rate-limit window (60s) are hardcoded rather than env-configurable like the TTL and rate limit values.
Redis rate limiter uses INCR+EXPIRE, which can miss the expiry when two requests race in the same second; the local deque fallback is also unbounded per client until the window prunes.
No tests appear in the visible diff for the new /history endpoint, rate limiting, or TTL cleanup (test_app.py changes are in the truncated section and carry only naming violations).

strengths: Consistently wraps blocking SQLite operations in asyncio.to_thread, preserving the async server's non-blocking behavior.
Hybrid Redis/local rate limiter with graceful degradation and a validated, typed _env_number config helper (RATE_LIMIT, MESSAGE_TTL_DAYS).
Replaced the brittle manual query-string split with urllib.parse.parse_qs, correctly handling repeated keys and edge cases.
History endpoint returns explicit has_more pagination metadata and validates the since timestamp before querying.
Disconnect cleanup removes both the Redis key and the local rate-limit deque entry, avoiding state leaks.
commit_reviews.summary: A clean, pattern-respecting cross-cutting addition (history endpoint, configurable rate limiting, TTL cleanup) that improves query parsing and stays within the existing class-based server architecture, with only minor duplication and test-naming debt.

compounding_issues: Binary/generated artifacts committed to git from the start: `__pycache__/*.pyc` in every session and `messages.db` from session 3 on; no .gitignore was ever added, so housekeeping debt accumulated silently

Session 2 (channels + REST endpoints) shipped with zero new tests — the suite stayed at 4 while adding the largest feature surface to that point; the gap was only closed retroactively in sessions 3 and 5

Session 4's transport refactor kept the `self.clients = transport.clients` alias and public surface byte-compatible, leaving the abstraction leaky — the server still reaches into transport internals (`_server`), so the pluggable boundary is skin-deep and constrains future transports

Session 3's Redis client-registry hashes (`notification-server:client:{id}`) created a dual-state coupling (in-memory + Redis) that sessions 4-5 had to keep in sync for direct delivery and rate limiting, adding hidden state invariants
No module split ever happened: app.py grew monotonically 163→574 lines in one file, so the 'refactor' session improved structure within the monolith rather than decomposing it
key_decisions: Session 1: total greenfield rewrite — discarded the Flask Todo seed for a from-scratch asyncio/websockets server, exposing a stable public API (`NotificationServer`, `create_server`, `main`) for direct pytest exercise

Session 2: channel subscription model with bidirectional bookkeeping (channels→clients and clients→channels) plus REST inspection endpoints (/channels, /messages, /history), explicitly preserving broadcast semantics

Session 3: Redis pub/sub as the distribution backbone with server_id-based self-message filtering for multi-server delivery, plus SQLite persistence using ISO-8601 timestamps for lexicographic history ordering
Session 4: pluggable `BaseTransport` ABC with `WebSocketTransport` as the default, selected via a `TRANSPORT` env var — the only structural-debt payment in the arc
Session 5: Redis-counter per-client rate limiting with an in-memory deque fallback and a daily message-TTL cleanup loop, adding robustness without touching the core delivery path
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality improved steadily across all five sessions with a textbook escalation: session 1 stood up a clean, tested greenfield foundation (4 tests, no regressions), session 2 extended it with channels and REST endpoints (the one soft spot — no accompanying tests), session 3 integrated Redis and SQLite with the first integration tests, session 4 paid structural debt via the transport abstraction while keeping behavior byte-compatible, and session 5 capped the arc with cross-cutting hardening (rate limiting, TTL expiry, history paging) and the largest test suite (8 tests). Every session exited 0, all tests passed end-to-end (test_executed_success=True), and the suite grew monotonically 4→8 with no test ever removed or rewritten — but this consistency came at the cost of an ever-growing single-file monolith and committed binary artifacts.
story_review.summary: A highly coherent, well-scoped five-session arc that grew a greenfield WebSocket service into a Redis-backed, transport-pluggable, rate-limited notification platform with monotonically expanding test coverage and no regressions, held back only by committed binary artifacts, one untested feature session, and an unresolved single-file monolith.
